column2: Eric Jorgenson

column1: Seek wealth, not money or status
column2: Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep. Status games are zero-sum; wealth creation is positive-sum.
Renting out your time caps your income. Owning a piece of a business lets your effort scale.
Your edge comes from curiosity-driven skills that feel like play to you and work to others.
Code, media, capital and people multiply your output. Code and media need no one's permission.
Trust, reputation and returns compound when you work with the same good people for years.
Being right about what to do matters more than how hard you work at it.
Reading for pleasure builds the habit. The habit builds the knowledge.
Peace comes from fewer desires, not more achievements. Train it like any other skill.

column1: Desire is a contract to be unhappy
column2: Each desire is a deal: you stay unhappy until you get the thing. Pick few.
Physical fitness and calm make every other goal easier. Protect them early.
Oliver Burkeman
An average life lasts about four thousand weeks. Accepting that limit sharpens your choices.

column1: You will never get it all done
column2: The inbox refills forever. Efficiency only brings more tasks, not freedom.
Saying yes to something means saying no to everything else. Make those trade-offs on purpose.
Keep only a few projects active. Finish one before starting the next.
Missing out is unavoidable. Joy comes from fully living the choices you do make.
Hard things take the time they take. Rushing creates anxiety, not speed.
Leisure doesn't need to justify itself as recovery for more work.
What you pay attention to, moment by moment, is what your life becomes.
Shared rhythms like meals and rituals make time feel richer than solo optimization.
Waiting for certainty means waiting forever. Start with an imperfect step.
Austin Kleon
Amateurs learn in public and share freely. You don't need to be an expert to help others.
Share the messy middle of your work, not just the polished end.
Little daily updates add up to a body of work people can follow.
Share what inspires you. Your influences reveal who you are.
Work doesn't speak for itself. Explain where it came from and why it matters.
Sharing your tricks doesn't kill your edge; it attracts people who value you.
Give more than you ask. Be a connector, not a broadcaster.
Criticism comes with visibility. Learn from it, or let it go.
Ask for support without shame. Making a living lets you keep making work.
Careers are long. Keep going through the quiet periods and keep starting over.
Cal Newport
Few people know their passion upfront. Following it blindly leads to job hopping.
Love for work often grows after you become very good at it.
Focus on what you can offer the world, not what the world owes you.
Rare and valuable skills are what you trade for great jobs.
Stretch beyond comfort and get honest feedback. Routine work doesn't grow skill.
Autonomy is a top reward, but you must earn the leverage to claim it.
Seeking freedom before you have skills leaves you with neither.
A unifying purpose usually appears at the edge of your field, after mastery.
Test mission ideas with cheap experiments before making big leaps.
Pursue projects that make people talk, in venues that spread them.
Steven Pressfield
An inner force fights every creative or growth-oriented act. Name it to beat it.
The more important a task is to your growth, the more resistance you'll feel.
Putting off creative work is the most common way resistance wins.
Amateurs wait for inspiration. Professionals show up every day regardless.
Sit down at the same time daily. Inspiration tends to find you working.
Criticism is about the work, not your worth. Keep producing.
Being afraid of a project often means it truly matters.
The clever excuses you invent are resistance in disguise.
Focus on the craft itself, not on applause or rewards.
Once you commit fully, unexpected support and ideas appear.
BJ Fogg
An action happens when all three meet at the same moment.
Motivation goes up and down. Design habits that work on low-motivation days.
Shrink the habit until it's almost too easy, like flossing one tooth.
Attach the new habit to something you already do: after I pour coffee, I will…
A quick feeling of success right after the action wires the habit in.
Habits form from feeling good, not from repetition alone.
Tiny habits expand on their own once they feel automatic.
When a habit fails, adjust the design instead of judging yourself.
Remove prompts and add friction to stop unwanted behaviors.
Small successes build confidence, which makes bigger changes possible.
Ryan Holiday
The ability to be steady and focused while the world spins is trainable.
Consume less news and noise. A quieter mind sees more clearly.
Journaling moves worries out of your head and onto the page.
The best decisions come from patience and reflection, not reaction.
Knowing what you stand for removes many daily dilemmas.
Old wounds drive present behavior. Understanding them brings calm.
Wanting more keeps you restless. Contentment is the path to peace.
Steady daily rhythms free the mind for deep work and presence.
Walking clears the head and sparks insight.
Rest is part of performance, not a sign of weakness.
Rob Fitzpatrick
People are polite. Asking "do you like it?" gets useless compliments.
Ask about their problems and habits, not your solution.

column1: Ask about specifics in the past
column2: When did you last do this? beats "Would you ever?"
The customer should do most of the talking in a learning conversation.
Praise is noise. Look for facts, commitments and money.
Real interest shows as time, reputation or cash, not kind words.
A real problem is one people already spend effort or money on.
Informal chats get more honest answers than formal meetings.
Before each conversation, decide what you most need to learn.
Talk to a specific group. Too broad an audience gives mixed signals.
Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson
That won't work is often just fear. Small teams can do things differently.
Long-term plans are mostly fiction. Decide what to do this week instead.
Ideas are cheap. Execution is what counts.
Limited time, money and people force creative, simple solutions.

column1: Build half a product, not a half-assed one
column2: Cut features ruthlessly and do the core really well.
They break focus and waste many people's time at once. Keep them rare.
Ship a solid solution now rather than a perfect one never.
Sharing what you know builds an audience that big rivals can't buy.
Only hire once you're overwhelmed doing the work yourself.
Protect long stretches of alone time to get real work done.
Donella Meadows

column1: A system is more than its parts
column2: Elements, connections and purpose together create behavior no part has alone.
A stock is what accumulates; flows fill or drain it. Watch both.
Balancing loops stabilize; reinforcing loops amplify growth or decline.
Slow feedback makes people overshoot, then overcorrect.
What a system actually does shows its real goal, whatever it claims.
When actors pull in different directions, pushing harder rarely works.
Small changes in rules, goals or information flows can shift a whole system.
Systems that survive shocks often look wasteful in good times.
People act sensibly with the information they have, which may still harm the whole.
Observe how it behaves before you try to change it.
